title.en: The Sage Asita's Prophecy to Suddhodana (Buddhacarita)
title.zh: 阿私陀仙人預言（佛所行讚）

region.en: The royal palace of Kapilavastu, city of the sage Kapila (modern Piprahwa, UP, India)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛王宮，仙人迦毘羅所居之城（今印度烏塔爾邦皮普拉赫瓦一帶）

texts.period: Sanskrit kavya, c. 2nd c. CE (Book I by Asvaghosha); Cowell translation 1894 (SBE 49)

source.work: The Buddha-karita of Asvaghosha, trans. E. B. Cowell, 1894 (Sacred Books of the East vol. 49, Buddhist Mahayana Texts, Part I)

summary.en: Hearing a heavenly voice in the path of the sky that Suddhodana's son is born for the sake of supreme knowledge, the aged seer Asita — skilled in signs and penances — comes to the Sakya palace; beholding the babe with the wheel-marked foot and webbed fingers, he smiles and then bursts into tears. Alarmed, the king begs to know the danger; but Asita's grief is for himself: the child will leave the kingdom, attain the highest truth and become a sun of knowledge delivering the distressed world from the ocean of misery — and Asita, who has mastered all the stages of contemplation, is doomed to die before he can hear that law. He charges the king's young nephew, and departs through the air.
summary.zh: 仙人阿私陀於天路聞空中有聲：釋種之子將誕，為求無上知故。乃以神通至迦毘羅衛王宮；觀嬰兒足有輪相、指間縵網，微笑而隨即垂淚。王驚惶叩問：兒有夭折之厄乎？仙答：非也，慮在己身——此子當捨王國、樂出家，以精勤得最上真諦，為世界智慧之日，破除痴暗，以智慧之舟載度苦海眾生；而我壽將盡，不能聞其法，縱生最上天界亦是苦。遂囑其妹之子諦聽斯言，騰空而去。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Having learned by signs and through the power of his penances this birth of him who was to destroy all birth, the great seer Asita, in his thirst for the excellent Law, came to the palace of the Sakya king. Him, shining with the glory of sacred knowledge and ascetic observances, the king's own priest introduced into the royal palace with all due reverence; and Suddhodana, having duly honoured the sage with water for the feet and an arghya offering, invited him to speak. 'I am indeed fortunate, this my family is the object of high favour, that thou shouldst have come to visit me; be pleased to command what I should do, O benign one; I am thy disciple.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book I (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sage, thus invited, uttered his deep and solemn words, his large eyes opened wide with wonder: hear the motive of my coming and rejoice — a heavenly voice has been heard by me in the heavenly path, that thy son has been born for the sake of supreme knowledge; I am come with a longing to see the banner of the Sakya race, as if it were Indra's banner being set up. The king, his steps bewildered with joy, took the prince from his nurse's side and showed him to the holy ascetic; and the great seer beheld him with wonder — his foot marked with a wheel, his fingers and toes webbed, a circle of hair between his eyebrows, and signs of vigour like an elephant's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book I (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: But beholding the babe seated on his nurse's side like the boy Skanda by Devi, the sage stood with tears hanging on his eyelashes, sighing, looking up to heaven. The king, agitated for his son, asked in a broken voice: is the prince destined to a long life? surely he cannot be born for my sorrow! Knowing his fear, the sage answered: let not thy mind be disturbed, all I have said is true — my grief is for mine own disappointment; it is my time to depart, and this child is born who knows the means of destroying birth. He will leave his kingdom and shine as a sun of knowledge to destroy the darkness of illusion; the thirsty world will drink the stream of his Law, and he will proclaim the way of deliverance to the lost. Make no sorrow for him; it belongs rather to the pitiable world of beings who refuse to hear his Law. Since I have fallen short of hearing it, though I have mastered all the stages of contemplation, I count even dwelling in the highest heaven a misfortune. Then the sage departed by the way of the wind as he had come.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book I (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The Palace Lament: Kanthaka's Neigh and Yasodhara's Grief (Buddhacarita)
title.zh: 宮中哀慟：馬嘶與耶輸陀羅之慟（佛所行讚）

region.en: Kapilavastu, the royal palace, the morning after the prince's flight
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛王宮，王子夜遁翌晨

texts.period: Sanskrit kavya, c. 2nd c. CE (Book VIII by Asvaghosha); Cowell translation 1894 (SBE 49)

source.work: The Buddha-karita of Asvaghosha, trans. E. B. Cowell, 1894 (Sacred Books of the East vol. 49, Buddhist Mahayana Texts, Part I)

summary.en: The charioteer Chandaka rides back the one-night road in eight days, leading the empty-saddled horse; the city bereft of the prince is a forest, and the crowds weep in the road accusing Chandaka, who answers that he and the householder's dress were abandoned together in the forest. Kanthaka enters the stable and neighs; the deceived women rush out in wild hope, then faint when they see the horse's empty back. Gautami falls like a golden plantain-tree; the women beat their breasts; and Yasodhara pours out her grief on the horse — three went away together and only two return — until the king recovers hope from the reading of the omens.
summary.zh: 車匿奉主命，一夜之路卻以八日返，牽空鞍之馬回城；城中失王子如曠野，眾人於道哭泣，責車匿竊王子；車匿答：非我棄主，乃主於林中將我與在家衣一併捨棄。健陟馬入廄嘶鳴，宮中婦女誤聞以為王子歸，狂喜奔出，見馬鞍空而昏絕。喬曇彌如失犢之母牛倒地；諸女捶胸慟哭；耶輸陀羅向馬致哀——三人同出，二人獨還——直至王觀其夢兆復生希望。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Meanwhile the attendant of the horse, in deep distress, when his unselfish master thus went into the forest, made every effort in the road to dissolve his load of sorrow, and yet not a tear dropped from him; but the road which by his lord's command he had traversed in one night with that horse, that same road he now travelled in eight days, pondering his lord's absence. And the horse Kanthaka, though he still went on bravely, flagged and had lost all spirit in his heart; and decked though he was with ornaments, he had lost all his beauty when bereft of his master. Slowly the two came back to the city called after Kapila, which seemed empty when deserted by that hero bent on the salvation of the world — like the sky bereft of the sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book VIII (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The men of the city, hearing that they had returned without the pride of the Sakya race, shed tears in the road and followed Chandaka crying, 'Where is the king's son, the glory of his race and kingdom? He has been stolen away by thee.' He answered that he had not left the king's son; but that by him, in the uninhabited forest, he, weeping, and the dress of a householder were abandoned together. The women crowded to the rows of windows crying 'The prince has returned'; but having heard that his horse had an empty back, they closed the windows again and wailed aloud. Then Kanthaka, entering the royal stable with eyes full of tears, uttered a loud sound as if uttering his woe to the people; the birds and horses re-echoed it, and the people near the king's inner apartments, deceived by excessive joy, thought 'Since the horse Kanthaka neighs, the prince must be coming.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book VIII (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The women who were fainting with sorrow now rose in wild joy and rushed out of the palace full of hope like flickering lightnings from an autumn cloud — undressed, unkempt, their eyes dimmed by tears; but when they saw Chandaka standing helpless and the horse, the noble women wept with pale faces like cows abandoned by the bull. The king's principal queen Gautami fell bursting into tears on the ground with outstretched arms, like a golden plantain-tree with trembling leaves; others stood senseless as if painted, or watered their bosoms with their tears; the noble women beat their breasts with their lotus-like hands. Then Yasodhara spoke, her voice choking: 'Leaving me helplessly asleep in the night, whither, O Chandaka, is the desire of my heart gone? While three went away together, my mind trembles.' She rebuked the horse that carried away her treasure when all were asleep — and could not have done so had it but neighed once — till the king, by the signs he read, bade her cling to hope again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book VIII (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

title.zh: 頻毘娑羅王磐陀山勸請（佛所行讚）

region.en: Mount Pandava near Rajagriha, capital of Magadha (modern Rajgir, Bihar)
region.zh: 摩揭陀國王舍城磐陀山（今印度比哈爾邦王舍城）

texts.period: Sanskrit kavya, c. 2nd c. CE (Books X-XI by Asvaghosha); Cowell translation 1894 (SBE 49)

source.work: The Buddha-karita of Asvaghosha, trans. E. B. Cowell, 1894 (Sacred Books of the East vol. 49, Buddhist Mahayana Texts, Part I)

summary.en: The mendicant prince enters Rajagriha on his alms-round, and the whole city is stilled as at the presence of Religion embodied. King Srenya (Bimbisara), told that this is the youth the brahmans foretold would attain supreme wisdom or empire, climbs Mount Pandava to find him and offers half his kingdom, alliance in war, or the old career of pleasure and sacrifice. The bodhisattva praises the king's friendship but preaches the vanity of pleasures — even Indra's throne did not satisfy Mandhatri — declares his fear of worldly objects like serpents and thunderbolts, and says he goes that very day to the seer Arada. The king folds his hands and asks only: when thou hast accomplished all thou hast to do, show hereafter thy favour towards me.
summary.zh: 出家王子入王舍城乞食，闔城肅然，如見宗教化身。摩揭陀王頻毘娑羅聞婆羅門所預言者至，登山見之，願分半國、許以兵助，又以享受現樂、祭祀升天相勸。菩薩謝其友誼，而說欲樂之虛誑——曼陀陀那王得帝釋半座猶不饜——自言畏世間諸欲，如畏毒蛇雷電；今日即往阿羅邏仙人處。王合掌敬禮，唯求一諾：汝願成滿之日，當來度我。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Having crossed the Ganges with its speeding waves, the prince went to Rajagriha with its beautiful palaces and five hills. On seeing him, he who was going elsewhere stood still, and he who was standing followed him; those who wore gay-coloured dresses were ashamed, those who were talking fell to silence, and no one indulged in an improper thought, as at the presence of Religion herself embodied. King Srenya, the lord of the Magadhas, beheld the immense concourse from his palace and asked the reason; a man told him: this is the son of the king of the Sakyas, he who was foretold by the Brahmans — he will either attain supreme wisdom or the empire of the earth. The king sent a follower after the mendicant, who, having received alms, retired to eat in fitting manner and ascended the mountain Pandava.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book X (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king, deep in veneration, started himself to go thither with a modest retinue, and beheld the Bodhisattva resplendent as he sat on his hams with subdued senses — as if the mountain were moving and he himself were a peak thereof, like the moon rising from the top of a cloud. Drawing nigh and sitting down on the clean dark-blue rock, he spoke: I have a strong friendship with thy family, come down by inheritance and well proved. When I consider thy widespread race, thy fresh youth and thy conspicuous beauty, whence comes this resolve, set wholly on a mendicant's life and not on a kingdom? Thy limbs are worthy of red sandal-wood perfumes; this hand is fit to protect subjects, it deserves not to hold food given by another. If thou desirest not thy paternal kingdom, then at least accept forthwith one half of my kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Books X-XI (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Self-possessed and unchanged, the son of Suddhodana answered that the determination was prompted by pure generosity and friendship. I have experienced the fear of old age and death, he said, and fly to this path of religion in my desire for liberation; I am not so afraid of serpents or thunderbolts or flames as of these worldly objects. These transient pleasures are the robbers of our happiness; there is no calamity in the world like pleasures. Kings who have obtained all the earth wish to conquer the other side of the ocean; when Mandhatri had obtained the half of Sakra's throne, he was still unsatisfied; Nahusha fell, unsatisfied with pleasures. Who would trust worldly objects, which passed from Bali to Indra and back again? I go this very day to the seer Arada, who proclaims liberation — happiness be to thee, O king; guard the earth by the noble, and guard thy royal powers and thine own religion. The king, folding his hands, replied: when thou hast accomplished all that thou hast to do, show hereafter thy favour towards me. Having given his firm promise, the bodhisattva proceeded to the Vaivamtara hermitage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book XI (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Mara's Assault and Defeat at the Bodhi Tree (Buddhacarita)
title.zh: 魔軍攻擊與潰敗（佛所行讚）

region.en: The root of the asvattha (Bodhi) tree at Uruvela, on the Neranjara (modern Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 優樓頻螺尼連禪河畔菩提樹下（今菩提伽耶）

texts.period: Sanskrit kavya, c. 2nd c. CE (Book XIII by Asvaghosha); Cowell translation 1894 (SBE 49)

source.work: The Buddha-karita of Asvaghosha, trans. E. B. Cowell, 1894 (Sacred Books of the East vol. 49, Buddhist Mahayana Texts, Part I)

summary.en: The whole world rejoices as the sage sits resolved to win the highest knowledge, but Mara, the enemy of the good law, is afraid: if the sage overcomes him, his realm becomes empty. Armed with the flower-bow and the five infatuating arrows he had never spared even the lovers among birds, he assaults the seated saint, then summons his monstrous host — with the faces of boars, tigers and elephants, trunks, headless bodies and blazing hair — while the heavens fail to shine, the earth shakes and the oceans heave. Clubs are paralysed, hurled rocks hang in the sky, embers fall as lotus-petals, serpents stand charmed; the sage sits like a lion among oxen. An invisible voice warns Mara not to weary himself against this Meru of resolution; the flower-armed god flees vanquished, and the night gleams out like a spotless maiden as flowers fall from a clear sky.
summary.zh: 聖者端坐誓取無上智，世間歡慶；魔王懼其道場空虛，乃持花箭、五欲矢，勸誘不遂，即召魔軍——獸面獠牙、提頭無身、髮中出火——諸天失色、地動海翻。魔軍或擲石中懸、或降火成蓮、或蛇凝如咒縛；聖者如牛群中之師子，不動不驚。空中無形之聲告魔王：此志如須彌，不可撼也，宜斂瞋歸寂。花箭之神敗退；夜空如無垢少女，天雨眾花，皎潔清淨。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: When the great sage sat down there with his soul fully resolved to obtain the highest knowledge, the whole world rejoiced; but Mara, the enemy of the good law, was afraid. He whom they call in the world Kamadeva, the owner of various weapons, the flower-arrowed, the lord of the course of desire — it is he whom they also style Mara the enemy of liberation. His three sons Confusion, Gaiety and Pride, and his three daughters Lust, Delight and Thirst, asked the reason of his despondency; he answered: this sage, wearing the armour of resolution and having drawn the arrow of wisdom with the barb of truth, intends to conquer my realms. While he stands within my reach and his spiritual eyesight is not yet attained, I will assail him to break his vow, as the swollen might of a river assails a dam.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book XIII (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Having seized his flower-made bow and his five infatuating arrows, he drew near to the root of the asvattha tree with his children, and addressed the calm seer preparing to cross the ocean of existence: 'Up, up, O thou Kshatriya, afraid of death! Follow thine own duty and abandon this law of liberation; that is a glorious path which has been followed by former leaders of men.' But when the Sakya saint, unheeding, did not change his posture, Mara discharged his arrow at him, setting his daughters and sons in front — the very arrow by which the god Sambhu was pierced with love for the daughter of the mountain. It was in vain: the arrow fell slack. Then Mara called to mind his own army, and his followers swarmed round wearing different forms and carrying arrows, trees, darts, clubs and swords — with the faces of boars, fishes, horses, tigers, bears and elephants, one-eyed, three-headed, with protruberant bellies, half-mutilated faces, yellow or smoke-coloured hair, clothed in leather or nothing at all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book XIII (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the heavens ceased to shine, the earth shook, a wind of intense violence blew, and the oceans were agitated; but the great sage remained untroubled, like a lion seated in the midst of oxen. One demon lifted his club and his arm was instantly paralysed; those who lifted stones and trees could not throw them and fell themselves; a shower of live embers became a shower of red lotus-petals through his boundless charity; those who spat serpents found them unable to strike near him; an arrow set in a bow gleamed but did not issue forth. Then a being of invisible shape and pre-eminent glory addressed Mara from the heavens: fire might lose its heat, water its fluidity, earth its steadiness, but never will this sage abandon his resolution — pity the great physician who labours for the remedy of knowledge. Having seen the unshaken firmness of the saint, Mara departed dispirited and broken in purpose, and his host fled in all directions like a hostile army whose camp has been destroyed; the heavens shone out with the moon like a maiden with a smile, and a sweet-smelling shower of flowers fell down wet with dew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book XIII (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The Name Sarvarthasiddha and the Reading of the Thirty-Two Signs (Romantic Legend)
title.zh: 命名一切義成與三十二相之觀相（普曜經傳）

region.en: Kapilavastu, capital of the Sakyas (modern Piprahwa, UP, India)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛城，釋迦族之都（今印度烏塔爾邦皮普拉赫瓦一帶）

texts.period: Chinese translation of a Sanskrit Lalitavistara-tradition text, c. 5th c. CE; Beal translation 1875

source.work: The Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, trans. Samuel Beal, 1875

summary.en: On the day of the babe's birth five hundred of everything came into being — Sakya princes and princesses, foals, white elephants, gardens and tribute-bearing embassies — and Suddhodana, seeing all things perfectly accomplished, names his son Sarvarthasiddha, 'perfect prosperity.' He then summons all the astrologers to cast the horoscope; reading the child against their sacred books, they declare him marked with the thirty-two signs of a great man: as a secular householder such a one becomes a universal monarch; as a religious recluse, a perfectly illuminated Tathagata — and they recite the signs one by one, from the level feet with the thousand-rayed circles to the netted fingers and the long arms.
summary.zh: 太子誕生之日，凡事五百同時而出——釋種五百王子、五百王女、駒馬、白象、林苑、進貢之使——淨飯王見諸事悉皆圓成，乃為太子命名曰一切義成（音薩婆達悉多）。隨後徵召國中相師占卜之士入宮觀相，參照其聖典，斷言：此兒具三十二相，大丈夫相；為在家者則為轉輪聖王，出家修道則為正遍知如來——相師乃一一數其瑞相：足下平滿、千輻輪相、指纖長、網縵指、臂長垂膝等。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: At this time there were five hundred Sakya princes born, of whom the Bodhisattva himself was by far the most illustrious; there were five hundred Sakya princesses born, of whom Yasodhara was chief; five hundred children born of the concubines, of whom Chandaka was chief; five hundred foals born of the royal white mares, of which Kantaka was chief; and five hundred white elephants appeared of themselves and went round the city. Five hundred lovely gardens appeared on each side of the city, five hundred merchant-men with gold, silver and precious stones arrived, and five hundred superb umbrellas and dishes of grain were sent as tribute by five hundred different princes — all with a view to conduce to the prosperity of the Bodhisattva.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. IX (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: Suddhodana, seeing that all these things were perfectly accomplished, thought with himself: what name shall I give my new-born child? — and reflected: since on the day of his birth all things were so perfectly accomplished, I will name him Sarvarthasiddha, 'perfect prosperity.' Then he opened his treasury and took a hundred lakhs of gold to offer to his child as he gave him the name, saying in a gatha: within the King's palace all things were entirely prosperous; therefore the young child's name shall be Sarvarthasiddha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. IX (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: Suddhodana then issued his commands that all the astrologers and fortune-tellers should repair to the palace to examine the child and cast his horoscope. The Brahmans with earnest purpose examined his appearance, comparing it with all that was explained in their sacred books, and addressed the king: what great fortune is yours! This child is indeed born a king of all that lives, for his body is marked by the thirty-two infallible signs of greatness; and of persons so marked there are two sorts — if secular, then universal monarchs; if religious, then perfectly illuminated Tathagatas. Asked to particularize, they recited the signs one by one: the sole of the foot perfectly level, with the thousand-rayed circles beneath; the fingers tapering and long; the heel round and smooth; the fingers and toes severally connected with a fine net-like membrane; the shoulders round as the king of stags; the hands, without stooping, reaching to the knees.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. IX (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

title.en: Devadatta's Wounded Goose and the Prince's Claim (Romantic Legend)
title.zh: 提婆達多射鵠與太子護生（普曜經傳）

region.en: The Kan-ku (diligent labour) garden at Kapilavastu, the princes' training ground
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛「勤學」苑，釋種王子習藝之地

texts.period: Chinese translation of a Sanskrit Lalitavistara-tradition text, c. 5th c. CE; Beal translation 1875

source.work: The Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, trans. Samuel Beal, 1875

summary.en: At twelve the prince, self-taught and surpassing the masters, amuses himself in the garden shooting; his cousin Devadatta wings a passing goose with an arrow fixed in its feathers, and sends messengers to claim it. The prince draws the arrow, anoints the wound with oil and honey, and answers: if the bird were dead it would be yours; living, you have no title to it. When Devadatta insists that skill of shooting made it his, the prince summons the wise ancients of the Sakyas to judge; a deva of the Suddhavasa heaven, disguised as an old man, delivers the ruling: he who nourishes and cherishes is the owner; he who shoots and destroys is the loser and the disperser — and all the ancients confirm it. The prince adds his reason: he keeps the bird as a sign that hereafter, arrived at perfection, he will thus receive and protect all living creatures.
summary.zh: 太子十二歲，自學諸藝，勝於諸師；於苑中習射。其從弟提婆達多射飛鵠貫翼，遣使索之。太子拔箭，以油蜜塗創，答曰：若鳥已死，當還；鳥若生存，汝無所取。提婆達多言：我以射術得之。太子乃請釋種耆老斷之；淨居天化為老者而入眾中，判曰：養護者為主，射殺者為失——眾老皆許。太子自道其故：護此鵠者，示我來日成道時，當如是攝受救護一切眾生。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Up to the time of his eighth year the Royal Prince grew up in the royal palace without any attention to study; but from his eighth year till his twelfth he was trained under the care of Visvamitra and Kshantadeva. Having completed twelve years and being perfectly acquainted with all the customary modes of enjoyment, it came to pass that he was visiting the Kan-ku garden, and amused himself by wandering in different directions, shooting with his bow and arrow at whatever he pleased, having separated himself from the other Sakya youths who were enjoying themselves in the several gardens. At this time a flock of wild geese, flying through the air, passed over the garden, on which the young man Devadatta, pointing his bow, shot one of them through the wing, leaving his arrow fixed in the feathers; the bird fell to the ground in the middle of the garden.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XII (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Royal Prince, seeing the bird thus transfixed with the arrow and fallen to the ground, took it with both his hands, and sitting down with his knees crossed rested it in his lap; and with his own soft and glossy hand, smooth and pliable as the leaf of the plaintain, holding it with his left hand, with his right he drew forth the arrow and anointed the wound with oil and honey. At this time Devadatta sent messengers to the Prince: Devadatta has shot a goose which has fallen in your garden; send it to him without delay. The prince answered: if the bird were dead, it would be right I should return it forthwith; but if it is not dead, you have no title to it. Devadatta sent again: whether the bird be living or dead, it is mine; my skill it was that brought it down — on what ground do you delay to send it me?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XII (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Prince Royal answered: the reason I have taken possession of the bird is this, to signify that in time to come, when I have arrived at the condition of perfection to which I tend, I shall thus receive and protect all living creatures; but if you still say the bird belongs not to me, go and summon all the wise and ancient men of the Sakya tribe and let them decide the question on its merits. At this time a certain deva belonging to the Suddhavasa heaven assumed the appearance of an old man, entered the assembly of the Sakyas, and spoke thus: he who nourishes and cherishes is by right the keeper and owner; he who shoots and destroys is by his own act the loser and the disperser. At once all the ancient men of the Sakyas confirmed the words of the would-be clansman, saying: verily, verily, it is as this venerable one says, with respect to the difference between Devadatta and the Royal Prince.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XII (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tournament for Yasodhara and the Bow of Sinhahanu (Romantic Legend)
title.zh: 選妃競藝與祖父神弓（普曜經傳）

region.en: The place of tournament outside Kapilavastu, on the day of the Arrow Festival
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛城外競藝之場，射箭節之日

texts.period: Chinese translation of a Sanskrit Lalitavistara-tradition text, c. 5th c. CE; Beal translation 1875

source.work: The Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, trans. Samuel Beal, 1875

summary.en: On the seventh day the Sakya youths go to the tournament, and the minister Mahanama proclaims that whoever wins the contest of skill and arms shall carry off his daughter Yasodhara as his prize. The prince sweeps the writing contest under the smiling umpire Visvamitra, then defeats the whole five hundred at figures under the master Arjuna, reciting the centenary scale of numeration and the atom-reckoning that runs to the sands of myriads of Ganges rivers. In the martial exercises he strings — without rising from his seat — the sacred bow of his grandfather Sinhahanu, which no Sakya can string, shoots through the iron target ten krosas off, pierces seven tala-trees and an iron boar into the ground to make the Arrow Well, and burns a sala-grove through seven water-jars, till all the youths surrender and the devas establish the Arrow Festival in heaven with the arrow Sakra has caught.
summary.zh: 競藝之日，大臣摩訶那摩立其女耶輸陀羅為彩：技勇之勝者得娶之。太子書藝勝五百釋種；算術上又敗算學大師阿耆那，能誦十進位數法與極微積聚之算，至恆河沙數。武藝之場，太子坐不離席即張其祖父師子頰供於天廟之神弓——釋種無能張者——射十由旬外鐵鼓，貫七多羅樹與鐵豬，箭入地成井（至今號箭井），又以燃箭貫七水甕而焚娑羅林；眾皆服輸。帝釋取其箭上天，諸天以此日為射箭節，至今為紀。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: On the seventh day all the Sakya youths of the five hundred families, with Siddartha at their head, went forth from the city to the place of tournament. At this time the great minister Mahanama, having caused his daughter Yasodhara to be adorned with every choice ornament, made this proclamation respecting the victor: whoever the victor may be in this contest of skill and of arms, he shall carry off this my daughter as his prize. Suddhodana and all the old Sakya lords arrived at the jousting place with countless crowds of young men and women, desirous to see the prince and the Sakya youths contest for the prize. First they competed in writing, with Visvamitra as umpire, who smiled gently, knowing the prince's incomparable skill: whatever writing or books there be among men, in heaven, or among the Gandharvas, Asuras or Garudas, the prince is able thoroughly to understand them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XIII (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then came the art of figures, with the eminent master Arjuna as umpire. The prince proposed a sum that one Sakya youth copied down but could not do; then two, then three, till all the five hundred copied it down and failed; and when they proposed in turn, the prince solved every question without error. In astonishment Arjuna uttered his praise — surely we have found a master of figures, able even to count the drops of the ocean — and asked whether he could recite the numeration of figures above a lakh. The prince began: a hundred hundred thousand is a koti, a hundred kotis an ayuta — and so through the whole centenary scale, up to the enumeration that proceeds by the sands of one Ganges, or two, and by the sands of myriads of kotis of Ganges rivers; and to the atom-reckoning, in which seven minute atoms of dust make one mote, and so up to the measures of a yojana — a sum that made even the master confess himself in utter confusion of mind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XIII (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then came the martial exercises. Ananda set an iron drum two krosas off as a target, Devadatta four, Nanda six, Mahanama eight, and Siddartha one of diamond-hardness ten krosas off; each struck his target in the midst, but could not go beyond. The prince bent the given bow till it broke, and asked for one fit for him, his grandfather Sinhahanu's bow, kept in a temple of the devas, which no Sakya could string. Brought to him, he strung it without rising from his seat and thrummed the string, a sound that filled the city with fear; then he shot through each target to the farthest, where his arrow disappeared in the distance. The assembled devas sang his future victory over Mara, Sorrow and Death, and showered flowers on him; and Sakra seized the arrow, wherefore the day of the Arrow Festival is observed among the devas to this time. Then he shot through seven tala-trees and an iron boar, his arrow entering the earth and making the spring called the Arrow Well; and with one sword-cut he felled seven trees. Every contest won, he rejoiced the heart of his father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XIII (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

title.en: Suddhodana's Seven Dreams and the Disguised Deva (Romantic Legend)
title.zh: 淨飯王七夢與化形梵士（普曜經傳）

region.en: The royal palace of Kapilavastu, on the night after the first omen
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛王宮，初見老相之夜

texts.period: Chinese translation of a Sanskrit Lalitavistara-tradition text, c. 5th c. CE; Beal translation 1875

source.work: The Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, trans. Samuel Beal, 1875

summary.en: Having seen the prince turn home from the old man on the road, Suddhodana doubles the palace pleasures — and the devaputra T'so-Ping, still bent on ripening the bodhisattva's resolve, that very night sends the king seven dreams: an imperial banner carried out of the east gate by innumerable crowds, the prince in chariots passing the south and west gates, a jewelled discus flying through the north gate, the prince beating a great drum in the middle of the four highways, a tower from whose top he scatters jewels to the four quarters, and six men outside the city weeping and tearing their hair. The court brahmans cannot interpret them; but T'so-Ping, disguised as a brahman at the gate, reads each dream — the prince's renunciation, omniscience, fearlessness, the turning of the wheel, the drum of preaching heard through the heavens, the scattering of the gems of the Good Law, and the discomfiture of the six heretical teachers — then vanishes; and the king, misreading the comfort, resolves only to multiply the enticements of the palace.
summary.zh: 王聞太子歸而問故，倍增宮中之樂。時化樂天子時時欲成太子出家之志，是夜以神力使王得七夢：無數人眾擎天帝幡出東門；太子乘象車出南門；乘四馬車出西門；寶珠飛空出北門；太子於四衢擊大鼓；太子登高樓散寶珠四方；六人於城外拔髮號泣。朝中相師不能解。化樂天子化為梵士立於門，自言能解王夢；乃一一解之：太子將捨俗出家；證一切智十力；得四無畏；轉法輪；法音上徹梵天；散法寶於四方；伏六師外道。言畢忽然不見；王聞之，愈增宮中聲色，欲以繫太子之志。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: It came to pass that the Devaputra T'so-Ping, still desiring to cause the prince to arrive at a resolution to become a religious recluse, by the exercise of his spiritual power on that very night caused Suddhodana to dream seven different dreams. As soon as the king had retired to his couch and fallen asleep, he dreamt that he saw a great imperial banner like that of Indra, around which were gathered innumerable crowds of people, who, lifting it and holding it up, proceeded to carry it through Kapilavastu and finally went from the city by the Eastern gate. The second dream was that he saw the prince riding in a royal chariot drawn by great elephants, passing through the Southern gate; the third, that the prince seated in a magnificent four-horsed chariot proceeded through the Western gate; the fourth, that a magnificently jewelled discus flew through the air and proceeded through the Northern gate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XV (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fifth dream was that he saw the prince sitting in the middle of the four great highways of Kapilavastu, holding in his hand a large mace and smiting therewith a large drum. The sixth was that he saw in the midst of Kapilavastu a high tower, on the top of which the Royal Prince was seated, scattering towards the four quarters of heaven countless jewels of every kind, which were gathered by the innumerable concourse of living creatures; and the seventh, that he beheld outside the city, not very far off, six men who raised their voices and wailed greatly, and with their hands plucked out the hair of their heads and flung it by handfuls on the ground. Suddhodana, awaking and recalling the visions, was greatly troubled, his hair standing erect and his limbs trembling; and he bade his ministers recite the dreams in the morning, and summoned all the Brahmans, interpreters of dreams, in the kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XV (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: The wise Brahmans could make nothing of them: we never before have heard such dreams, they said. At this T'so-Ping assumed the appearance of a Brahman arrayed in the skin of the black deer, and standing at the gate of the palace cried out: I am able fully to interpret the dreams of Suddhodana and to satisfy all his doubts. Brought into the presence, he read each dream in turn: the banner carried from the city signifies that the prince will soon give up his present condition and, surrounded by devas, become a recluse; the elephants' car, his omniscience and the ten powers; the jewelled discus, his turning of the wheel of the perfect Law; the drum, that the sound of his preaching shall extend through the heavens of Brahma; the scattered jewels, his dispersal of the gems of the Good Law; the six weeping men, the distress of the six heretical teachers whom the prince shall discomfit. Then he said: your heart should be filled with joy, for these dreams are most felicitous — and suddenly disappeared, and was no more seen. The king thereupon resolved to multiply still further the palace enticements, hoping to prevent his going forth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XV (Beal 1875); not verbatim.
